title: Old Skomuck and the Pima chants on the reservation
summary: Moore recalls going as a six-year-old with other children to hear an elderly man, Skomuck, sing Pima chants and tell tribal stories; this was his first awakening to music.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Ok. Russell, could you tell us -- start by telling us something of your early life? You were born on the Pima Reservation at Komatkee, Gill Crossing.
Could you tell us something of your early life and childhood there, your earliest involvement -- leading to your earliest involvement in music.

Yes. The best of my recollection, I've always been musical ever since first awakenings about when I was about six years old when I used to go to an old man by the name of Skomuck on the reservation. He was in his ninties,

and a bunch of us kids would bring different gifts like maybe a sack of beans, corn, tobacco, and we'd go over and listen to him sing the chants of the Pimas. And we would listen to the stories of the early days of Pima land in early years when they used to -- the tribe used to fight with the Apaches, and the Pimas would fight with the Apaches and the constant turmoil there in the old days. And where the music part comes in is they have -- the Indians have songs that were depicted through battle songs, and I think everybody -- everyone in the early years is always -- have some conection with rhythm, melody. And even the -- go back to the Black tribes of -- African tribes, they have beautiful rhythm and song. And I can vouch for my tribe. We had rhythm and song too. And when we visited old Skomuck, we would just, out of respect for an old man who, who still followed the tribal chants and things like we, we would sit around close to him, and he would sing to us. That's the first time when I was six years old that I heard the chants of the Pima. And to this day, in all these years, I can still hear old Skomuck laying in his house on a blanket and treating us to his chants and his stories of Indian folklore. And that was my first awakening of music in my soul 'cause, as I said, to this day I can still sing the chants that old Skomuck used to sing to us kids. And one time we were at Skomuck listening to his singing and his chanting, and he kept us so long that we were -- we wouldn't tell him to stop, we're going home. We just
silently stole out of his adobe house, and we could still hear him although we were far away out to in our home. And we had quite a, quite a lot of experience with old Skomuck.
